Her complexion altered, and she fell silent.

Mrs. Gardiner stood a little to the rear. When Elizabeth paused, he asked whether she would grant him the honour of an introduction to her friends. She was wholly unprepared for such courtesy, and could scarcely keep from smiling to find him seeking the acquaintance of the very people whose existence had offended his pride when he proposed to her. “How astonished he will be,” she thought, “when he discovers who they are! At present he supposes them fashionable people.”

She made the introductions at once, however. As she explained their connection to herself, she glanced covertly at him to observe his reception of it, half expecting him to escape as quickly as possible from such discreditable company. His surprise at the relationship was plain, but he bore the discovery bravely. Instead of departing, he turned to accompany them and began talking with Mr. Gardiner. Elizabeth could not help feeling both pleasure and triumph. It comforted her that he should discover she possessed relations of whom she had no reason to be ashamed. She attended closely to everything the two men said, taking pride in each phrase and sentence from her uncle that displayed his understanding, refinement, or courtesy.

Their talk soon came round to fishing. She heard Mr. Darcy invite him, most politely, to fish there whenever he pleased during his stay in the neighbourhood. He also offered to provide tackle and indicated the stretches of the stream that generally afforded the best sport. Walking arm in arm with Elizabeth, Mrs. Gardiner gave her a glance full of astonishment. Elizabeth remained silent, but the attention pleased her greatly; she herself must be the object of the compliment. Yet her amazement was no less powerful. Again and again she asked herself, “Why has he changed so much? What can have caused it? Surely it cannot be for me, cannot be on my account, that his manners have grown so gentle. My reproaches at Hunsford could never have produced such an alteration. He cannot possibly still love me.”

They continued for some time in this order, the ladies leading and the gentlemen following. After they had gone down to the river's edge to examine an unusual water plant more closely, a slight rearrangement occurred as they resumed their walk. Mrs. Gardiner brought it about: tired by the morning's exercise, she found Elizabeth's arm insufficient support and chose her husband's instead.

We grew up together, with less than a year between our ages. I hardly need to say that disagreements and quarrels were unknown to us. Our companionship was perfectly harmonious, and the differences in our characters only brought us closer. Elizabeth was calmer and more inwardly settled. Yet despite my excitable nature, I could work with greater intensity, and my hunger for knowledge was much stronger. She loved to follow the poets' flights of imagination. The grand and wonderful landscape around our Swiss home gave her endless things to admire and enjoy: the magnificent mountains, the changing seasons, storms and stillness, winter's silence, and the busy, overflowing life of our Alpine summers. While she gazed at these splendid sights with thoughtful satisfaction, I took pleasure in discovering what caused them. To me, the world was a secret waiting to be understood. Some of my earliest memories are of curiosity, determined efforts to uncover nature's hidden laws, and an almost ecstatic joy whenever they became clear to me.

When my parents had a second son, seven years younger than I was, they gave up traveling altogether and settled in their native country. We owned a house in Geneva and a country home at Belrive, on the lake's eastern shore, a little over three miles from the city. We lived mostly at the country house, where my parents led a rather secluded life. By nature I preferred to avoid crowds and form deep attachments to a few people. Most of my schoolmates therefore meant little to me, but one became my closest friend. Henry Clerval was the son of a Geneva merchant, a boy with unusual talent and imagination. He loved daring projects, hardship, and even danger for its own sake. He had read widely in stories of knights and romance. He wrote heroic songs and began many tales of magic and knightly adventure. He tried to persuade us to perform plays and dress up as characters drawn from the heroes of Roncesvalles, King Arthur's Round Table, and the knights who shed their blood to recover the holy tomb from those they regarded as unbelievers.

No one could have enjoyed a happier childhood than mine. My parents were kindness and generosity itself. We never thought of them as tyrants who would govern our lives according to a passing whim. Instead, we saw them as the people who created and provided all the many pleasures that filled our days.

He was a small man, though strikingly upright, and his voice was sweeter than any I had heard. To begin his lecture, he reviewed the history of chemistry and the advances contributed by its various scholars, speaking the names of the greatest discoverers with enthusiasm. He then briefly surveyed the science in its present condition and clarified many of its basic expressions. Having performed a few introductory experiments, he ended with a tribute to modern chemistry whose language I can never forget:

“The earliest teachers of this science,” he said, “offered impossible promises and achieved nothing. Its modern masters promise little. They understand that metals cannot be transformed into one another and that the elixir of life is a fantasy. Yet these philosophers, whose hands appear fitted only for grubbing in dirt and whose eyes seem intended only to peer at crucibles and through microscopes, have accomplished wonders. They enter nature's most secret chambers and reveal her hidden operations. They rise into the heavens; they have learned the circulation of the blood and the character of the air we breathe. They have won fresh powers, almost without limit. They can summon heaven's thunder, imitate earthquakes, and even confront the unseen world with images of its own shadows.”

These were the professor's words—or rather, the words pronounced by fate for my destruction. As he continued, I seemed to feel my soul wrestling with a tangible foe. One after another, the keys governing the instrument of my being were struck; chord followed chord, until one thought, one idea, one intention occupied my whole mind. Much has already been accomplished, cried Frankenstein's soul; I shall accomplish more, infinitely more. Following the path others have traced, I shall open a new road, investigate unsuspected powers, and reveal to mankind the profoundest secrets of creation.

That night I never closed my eyes. My inner life was all rebellion and confusion. I sensed that order would emerge from it, but could do nothing to bring that order about. Only gradually, after dawn, did I fall asleep. When I woke, the thoughts of the previous night seemed dreamlike. What remained was a firm decision to resume my former studies and give myself to a science for which I believed I had a natural gift. I visited M. Waldman that same day. In private he was still gentler and more engaging than before. A certain stateliness had marked his bearing during the lecture; at home it gave way to the utmost friendliness and kindness.
